extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, AMS membership, mathematical community and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and evaluative standards about what constitutes significant mathematical work, how mathematics should interact with other sciences and institutions, and what policies/actions will help the field flourish in the coming decades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance via solution of famous problems
rubrics_metrics.description: "The solution to historically famous problems is considered significant. Nobody in the mathematical world could doubt that Fermat's Last Theorem and the Riemann Hypothesis are of high significance. The same can be said for the 'Millennium Prize Problems'..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the settlement of long-standing, celebrated problems (e.g., Fermat, Riemann, Clay Millennium Problems) as one axis for judging importance; such problems are plausible candidates for being considered significant even if not the only route to importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bisociation (creativity from unexpected unions)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Bisociation occurs when two seemingly unrelated things are shown to have unanticipated connections... 'it is by unexpected union between its diverse parts that it progresses.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize and value work where ideas/techniques from one area impinge fruitfully on another (examples: Atiyah–Singer Index theorem, Donaldson's use of quantum field theory in topology, Witten's interplay of QFT and topology, the Langlands Program). Bisociation is presented as a major criterion for future significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary impact with sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics' most important bisociation lies in the interaction between mathematics and the sciences (computer science, physics, molecular biology, genomics, data analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate and encourage mathematical work that meaningfully connects to and advances scientific domains (e.g., computational complexity, coding/number theory, genomics data analysis, wavelets in data analysis). External scientific problems are a major source of important mathematical developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centrality of computing and computational considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: "Everything that relates to [the computer] sphere will be of central importance to mathematics in the coming century... The influence of quantum computation is hard to predict... But many other things—such as complexity of computation or number theory applied to codes—provide very striking examples..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how mathematical work addresses computational complexity, coding theory, algorithms, or prospective areas like quantum computation; computing-related directions are high-priority growth areas even when outcomes are uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of new mathematical frameworks applied to existing fields (e.g., Malliavin Program)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples where techniques from one field (Sobolev spaces for PDEs) are applied to another (stochastic processes or topology), e.g., the Malliavin Program putting stochastic processes in the framework of Sobolev spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and reward methodological transfers that open new avenues in established fields; such transfers may reshape how a subject is practiced and judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity and specialization balanced with cross-field interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is now extremely diverse; many people work on narrow subjects. Yet significant developments often arise when diverse parts interact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While specialization is a historical reality, evaluate proposals and careers favoring both depth and mechanisms (training, conferences, collaborations) that facilitate cross-disciplinary contact and bisociation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical attempts to set agendas can stimulate research
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert's attempt to set the course (Hilbert Problems) did not predict everything but greatly stimulated research and diversified mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the pragmatic value of formulating grand challenges or problem lists—even if predictions are imperfect—as tools to stimulate and organize research activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against overformalization/axiomatization of domains like physics
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert's problem to axiomatize physics was 'a misguided endeavor' because physics changed drastically (relativity, quantum theory); axiomatization may be brittle in rapidly changing sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of pursuing overly rigid formalization of rapidly evolving scientific domains; emphasize adaptability and empirical awareness when trying to import axiomatic programs into applied sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of data analysis and modern statistical/mathematical tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical rituals of statistics no longer suffice for many problems, especially with large masses of data; sophisticated tools (e.g., wavelets) are being used in data analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value research and training that develops or applies modern mathematical tools for big-data problems and modern statistical challenges; classical statistical methods may be inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional engagement and policy advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians have to be aware and alert in responding when problems arise in institutions that determine our destiny. The AMS is playing an important role in organizing and focusing attention on policy matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage active participation in institutional/policy processes (attend AMS/committee meetings, engage with government and funding agencies) and support societies that advocate for mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vigilance toward education and political threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: French minister Claude Allègre advocated eliminating mathematics classes—illustrating mathematicians must be alert and respond when such policy threats arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include public advocacy and defense of mathematics education as part of professional responsibilities; monitor and counter misguided policy proposals affecting math education and research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding and recruitment as decisive constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics in the United States is flourishing but not guaranteed to continue: scarcity of resources and, even more important, scarcity of recruitment—especially talented American students—are crucial questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate plans and policies by how well they address funding sustainability and talent recruitment; programs should prioritize attracting and training new generations of mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convene focused meetings to identify challenges and directions
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizing symposia (e.g., 'Mathematical Challenges of the 21st Century') along particular axes (such as bisociation) is a productive way to think about and stimulate future directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conferences/symposia curated around thematic axes to spotlight promising cross-disciplinary directions and to catalyze collaborative programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability of students and practitioners to shifting trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Students have learned to adapt to such changes; sometimes they 'flock from one fad to another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and foster flexibility in training and career planning so mathematicians can respond to emerging problems and interdisciplinary opportunities rather than remaining narrowly fixed.
